destination.title: Following the deposit rule is what made her a suspect

short35: You run a cash business.
You follow every rule.
And the government empties your bank account
without ever charging you with a crime.
Carole Hinders ran a small
cash-only restaurant in Iowa for decades.
She deposited her earnings at the bank
in amounts under ten thousand dollars.
For that alone
the I-R-S seized her entire account
nearly thirty-three thousand dollars.
It's called structuring
deliberately splitting deposits to dodge the bank's
ten-thousand-dollar reporting rule.
But she committed no other crime
and every dollar was honest restaurant income.
Under civil forfeiture
the government took it first and made
her fight to get it back.
As cases like hers drew national attention
the I-R-S announced it would stop seizing
money from people with no criminal case.
Carole's money was returned
and Congress later passed a reform to
curb the practice.
Watch the full story on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: There is a banking rule almost nobody bothers to explain.
It was never aimed at a cash register in a diner.
That last question — whether the government should be watching an ordinary cash business in the first place — is one almost no one in power stops to ask, and it hangs over everything that follows.
She has said she never knew banks reported large deposits at all.
For most of those thirty-eight years, none of this touched her.
The thirty-eight years, the sales rung up one plate at a time, none of it entered into it, because in a case against money, the person barely appears at all.
Not a courtroom, not a ruling that she was innocent, a reporter, a front page, and a national audience, a run of luck that almost nobody in her position ever gets.
The seizure had come first, and the agency's own change of heart never reached it.
The justice Carole never got, he did, the same law, the same innocence, opposite endings, decided almost entirely by the procedural wording of how each case was closed.
His money came back in the summer of two thousand fifteen, and the ruling in his favor read almost like an apology the government would never say out loud.
One day, on a slow Tuesday you never saw coming, it could be reaching for yours.
By her lawyers' account, she had already sold the restaurant — and she never got the year back.
era_note: 2013-2019 small-town America — an Iowa cash restaurant, a North Carolina country convenience store, bank counters, a Treasury audit and a congressional hearing room. Present-day stock reads correctly; nothing here is period.

shorts.angle: Two owners caught by the same structuring theory ended opposite ways: a store owner in North Carolina was paid his fees, costs and interest, while Carole Hinders was told she had not substantially prevailed.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Why two words in a dismissal order decided which of them the law would make whole.
shorts.loop_join: L8's 'she won, and still paid to win' closes the split L1 opens with — the same law, one owner's fees paid, the other's not.

lines.text: Two people, the same law, the same argument that the money was clean. One got his legal fees paid. The other got nothing.
source_lines: Two people, McLellan and Carole, caught by the same law, making the same argument, that the money was clean and the seizure was wrong.
The justice Carole never got, he did, the same law, the same innocence, opposite endings, decided almost entirely by the procedural wording of how each case was closed.

lines.text: In Fairmont, North Carolina, a man named Lyndon McLellan ran a country convenience store. The government seized his entire business account.
source_lines: In Fairmont, North Carolina, a man named Lyndon McLellan ran a country convenience store. The government seized one hundred seven thousand, seven hundred two dollars and sixty-six cents from him — his entire business account, over the same theory that had been used on Carole.

lines.text: One hundred seven thousand, seven hundred two dollars and sixty-six cents. Three hundred one deposits. Two million dollars in sales over three years.
source_lines: Three hundred one deposits. Around two million dollars in legitimate sales, rung up over three years, every one of them under ten thousand dollars.

lines.text: His store ran on gas, cigarettes and lottery tickets, a few dollars at a time. That ordinary shape was read as a scheme.
source_lines: His store was the kind of place that runs on small transactions — gas, cigarettes, lottery tickets, a few dollars at a time — which meant his deposits were naturally, unavoidably small. The very shape of an ordinary rural business was what the government read as a scheme.

lines.text: McLellan's money came back in 2015, and a judge ordered the government to pay his legal fees, his costs, and interest on top.
source_lines: His money was returned, and a judge ordered the government to pay his legal fees, his costs, and interest on top.
His money came back in the summer of two thousand fifteen, and the ruling in his favor read almost like an apology the government would never say out loud.

lines.text: Carole's case was dismissed too, but the government dismissed it without prejudice, walking off the field instead of admitting it had lost.
source_lines: Because the government had dismissed her case that way, walking off the field instead of admitting it lost, a federal appeals court ruled, in two thousand sixteen, that Carole had not substantially prevailed.

lines.text: In 2016 a federal appeals court ruled she had not substantially prevailed. She got her money back, but not her legal fees.
source_lines: In plain terms, it means this: she got her money back, but she was not entitled to her legal fees.

lines.text: She had been forced to spend to defend savings that were hers the entire time. She won, and still paid to win.
source_lines: She had been forced to spend to defend savings that were hers the entire time, and now she would swallow that cost too. She won, and still paid to win.

shorts.avoids: Short 35 told Carole's seizure and return; this cut is the second owner, the numbers behind his case, and the fee ruling that separated them.

shorts.angle: A Treasury watchdog measured these structuring seizures and found nine in ten of the traceable cases involved money from legal sources, which made her a representative case rather than an unlucky one.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What it finally took to close the specific trap that number exposed, and how much of the power survived.
shorts.loop_join: L8 says the watchdog's own files said so in a single number, which is the ninety-one percent L1 opens with.

lines.text: A federal watchdog pulled the files on these seizures. Where the money could be traced, ninety-one percent came from legal sources.
source_lines: A federal watchdog inside the Treasury Department pulled the records on these structuring seizures. In a sample of two hundred seventy-eight cases where investigators could actually trace where the money came from, ninety-one percent of those cases involved money from legal sources.

lines.text: The sample was two hundred seventy-eight traceable cases. Across more than two hundred of them, the government took around seventeen million dollars.
source_lines: Across more than two hundred of those cases, the government had taken in around seventeen million dollars from people whose money it could not tie to any crime.

lines.text: From people whose money it could not tie to any crime. Nine in ten. Ordinary businesses, like a diner, like a store.
source_lines: Nine in ten. Ordinary businesses, like hers, like McLellan's.

lines.text: That number changes what this is about. The seizures were not catching criminals who slipped through. They flagged a pattern and took money.
source_lines: That number changes what all of this is really about. If nine of every ten owners caught in this net turned out to be running clean businesses, then the seizures were not catching criminals who slipped through.

lines.text: And then waiting to see who could afford to fight back. The tax agency had announced it would stop taking legal-source accounts.
source_lines: The system was working as designed — flagging the pattern, taking the money, and waiting to see who could afford to fight back.

Around the same time the pressure was building, the tax agency had signaled a change of its own: going forward, it would generally stop seizing money in cases like hers, where the cash came from a plainly legal source.

lines.text: A policy memo is not a law. It is an instruction the agency writes to itself, and nobody outside the agency could enforce it.
source_lines: And a policy memo is not a law. It is an instruction the agency writes to itself — one it can read narrowly, apply unevenly, or set aside when it decides a case is different. Nobody outside the agency voted on it. Nobody could enforce it.

lines.text: For a while, seizures like hers kept happening anyway. Words on a page do not reach a case already open in a field office.
source_lines: And for a while, seizures like hers kept happening anyway.
But a memo is only words on a page, and words on a page do not always reach a case already sitting open in a field office in another part of the country.

lines.text: She was not an unlucky exception. She was a representative case, and the watchdog's own files said so in a single number.
source_lines: Carole was not an unlucky exception. She was a representative case.
